claims.text: A Role is a namespaced object holding rules; each rule lists apiGroups, resources and verbs, and the Role grants those permissions only within its own namespace.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Reference > API Access Control > Using RBAC Authorization (Role and ClusterRole)

claims.text: A rule allows every combination of the API groups, resources and verbs it lists.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Using RBAC Authorization (Role examples; PolicyRule in the RBAC API reference)

claims.text: A RoleBinding grants the permissions of a Role to a list of subjects (users, groups) and must be in the same namespace as the Role it references; a Role bound by nothing grants nothing.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Using RBAC Authorization (RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding: 'A RoleBinding may reference any Role in the same namespace')

claims.text: RBAC permissions are purely additive (no deny rules): a request is allowed if a rule from a binding of the user or one of its groups, in the request's namespace, matches its API group, resource and verb; otherwise the API server answers 403.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Using RBAC Authorization (Role and ClusterRole: 'Permissions are purely additive (there are no "deny" rules)')

claims.text: To remove a right granted by RBAC you remove or narrow the binding (or the Role) that grants it; another Role cannot subtract it.
claims.source_hint: follows from claim 4; kubernetes.io Using RBAC Authorization

claims.text: Opinion: least privilege in RBAC works by leaving actions out — grant only the verbs, kinds of objects and namespaces the work needs — because a too-wide grant cannot be narrowed later by another rule.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Concepts > Security > Role Based Access Control Good Practices (Least privilege)

claims.text: An API group is a named set of resource kinds; Pods and Secrets are in the core group, written as "" in apiGroups. Resources are written as the plural lower-case resource name, such as pods.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Using RBAC Authorization (Role example: apiGroups [""] indicates the core API group; Referring to resources)

claims.text: Verb get reads one named object, list reads a collection, watch follows changes to objects.
RoleBinding syntax: subjects entries with kind User, name, apiGroup rbac.authorization.k8s.io; roleRef with kind Role and name pod-reader (and apiGroup). Users are not objects in the cluster.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Using RBAC Authorization (RoleBinding examples; Referring to subjects)

claims.text: List and watch on Secrets return full objects including data, so granting them lets the caller read values; kubectl -o jsonpath='{.items[*].data}' only formats the data field of the items in the list response.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Concepts > Security > RBAC Good Practices (Listing secrets); kubectl reference: JSONPath support; outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/rbac-role.txt

claims.text: A Pod can use any Secret in its own namespace as an environment variable or volume files, so someone who may create Pods there can expose a Secret's value without RBAC rights on Secrets; keeping a Secret out of that namespace avoids it.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: RBAC Good Practices (Workload creation); Concepts > Configuration > Secrets (Information security for Secrets: a user who can create a Pod that uses a Secret can see its value)

claims.text: Encrypting Secret data in etcd protects the stored data (e.g. etcd files and backups); the API server decrypts it when serving requests, so callers authorized to read Secrets still get the value.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Tasks > Administer a Cluster > Encrypting Confidential Data at Rest (what it protects; data decrypted when read through the API)

claims.text: Secret values are base64-encoded, an encoding and not encryption; base64 -d recovers the value.

donhang-staging is created by scripts/devops/tofu-env.sh staging up (the second argument is mandatory); rbac-role.sh creates security-lessons itself (line 9) and leaves the Role and RoleBinding in place.

claims.text: Authentication supplies a user's groups together with its user name, from the same credential (e.g. the organization fields of a client certificate, or the groups attached to a token).
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Reference > API Access Control > Authenticating (Users in Kubernetes; X509 client certificates; Static token file)

claims.text: kubectl create ... --dry-run=client -o yaml only prints the object without sending it to the cluster; piping it to kubectl apply -f - creates the object.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: kubectl reference (kubectl create secret generic --dry-run; kubectl apply)
